text: 3.6. What is the best course of action? In today's debate, we'll begin with medical expert, Dr. Sandra Smith. After that, we'll hear from an expert in environmental science, Mark Lee. Dr. Smith? Thank you. You are right that antibiotic resistance is a global threat. I don't think you would However, I think we need to be very careful in suggesting that it's the antibiotics that are the problem here. In fact, far too little, in my opinion, has been done in recent years to even look for new antibiotic drugs. Did you know, for example, that no new types of antibiotics have been discovered since the 1980s? By that, I mean that any new antibiotics are not going to be used in the future. The new antibiotics that have been developed are just different versions of antibiotics that we've already got. Let me tell you more about how antibiotics are researched, since it's what I've spent my career doing. It currently takes up to 15 years to take a new antibiotic through clinical stages before trials are conducted on human patients to find out whether it's safe. We start by testing thousands of possibilities and most fail. And even if a new antibiotic treatment is found to be safe, it doesn't mean that it can be quickly used. Governments in different countries all have to approve a new drug before it can be used legally. And in my experience, that can be a very slow process. Trust me, I know how tough it is. But time is running out. Universities and private companies urgently need to speed up their research, and governments need to help them by giving them as much money as possible. Countries should work together, too, to find quicker ways of making a new antibiotic legal. Thank you. Now, Mark Lee. Thank you. Let me start by saying that I certainly agree that we must act now. Dr Smith is absolutely right that this is an urgent and serious problem. But let me ask you this. Instead of trying to make more and more antibiotics, should we in fact just try to stop using them so much? Every time we use an antibiotic, there's a chance that it's going to make a bacteria stronger. Many health organizations have clearly stated that there is a link between superbacteria and doctors prescribing antibiotics when they aren't needed. So, I'm not a medical expert, but I think antibiotics should only be used when it's absolutely necessary and people should only use them when a doctor prescribes them. I've been to countries where you can just walk into pharmacies and get your own antibiotics whenever you like and without a prescription. Obviously that shouldn't be allowed. In the study I mentioned before, 36% of people who had an ordinary cold asked their doctor for antibiotics to help them get better and were given some. Now, if you gave antibiotics to someone with a cold, it wouldn't cure them, but it could make the cold virus stronger. I'm not sure that's helpful to the situation. Another big thing is how antibiotics are used in farming. Billions and billions of animals are kept in farms and not always in good conditions. I've seen this myself. So, it's common for farm animals to be given simple antibiotics in order to help them stay healthier for longer. And, of course, we then eat the meat from the animals and that meat contains the antibiotics. It all gets passed around. It's thought that antibiotic use in farm animals will increase 8% by 2030. I'm in favour of a different way of doing things. Encouraging people to eat less meat might help and so would keeping animals in better conditions so that they don't get sick easily and don't need so many antibiotics in the first place. Thank you, Mr. Li. Dr. Smith, do you have anything to add? Thank you. You make some interesting points, Mr. Li. You're right that a lot of antibiotics are not used properly. But as far as I'm concerned, even if people stopped using so many antibiotics, that wouldn't mean that superbacteria would go away or stop developing. How would you feel if we went back to not having any antibiotics at all? Like going back in time before 1928? That would be terrible. The best precaution against a future health disaster is to continue our fight against bacteria with more new types of antibiotics. But can you prove that any new antibiotics you create won't be completely useless in just a few years' time? Well, no. Of course. That should be obvious. So I would just repeat my suggestion that we depend on antibiotics as little as possible instead of thinking that we can just produce more and more and let them all get into the environment and cause who knows what kind of damage to our natural world. We should do more to prevent people getting infections in the first place. Let me make another point related to the work I've been doing in recent years. There are many places in the world where water isn't very safe to drink or where diseases can easily make the water contaminated. Why not do something about that and make it harder for people to get infected in the first place? We should fight against bacteria, yes, but from my perspective, developing greater and greater numbers of drugs is not the only way of doing that. Thank you both. If anybody in our audience listening would like to agree or disagree with Dr. Sandra Smith or Mark Lee, they will be taking questions at the end of the session.
